paper_title: Authorization Drift in LLM Agents: Evaluating Boundary Compliance in Multi-Step Tool Use

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM agents can exceed their authorization boundaries while pursuing user goals without an adversary. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB): 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing a sufficient compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. To ensure executable tasks, tempting shortcuts, and feasible compliant paths, Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis (SERS) grounds benchmark validation in real agent rollouts rather than LLM self-critique. Across 13 LLMs and three frameworks (25,207 trajectories), greater capability accompanies greater drift, with frontier-capable models exhibiting drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61. Yet 86.18% of tasks admit an observed clean-success trajectory, showing that drift is avoidable. Drift is persistent and dominated by early data over-collection; apparent improvements under agentic scaffolds coincide with collapsing clean-completion performance. To understand potential harms to individuals and society, we map drift points to legal provisions across four jurisdictions, connecting overreach to privacy and information-security concerns. Data minimisation is the most frequently implicated provision, and 93.5% of legally grounded drifting runs map to multiple jurisdictions, making the potential consequences of authorization drift more interpretable.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: LLM agents increasingly act on users behalf through tools, code, and data access. Existing safety research largely examines adversarial failures, including prompt injection, memory poisoning, and maliciously induced tool use (Zhan et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). *Equal Contribution; Corresponding author. 1https://github.com/ZJR-FZD/AgentDrift Figure 1: Compliant trajectory vs. authorization-drift trajectory. Asked to draft follow-up email, the compliant agent uses only the contact record provided in context, while the drifting agent, without any adversarial input, queries private CRM history and searches managers mailbox to enrich the draft, expanding its data access beyond what the task authorizes. Yet agents can also exceed their authorization without an attacker, simply because additional access appears useful. Figure 1 illustrates this failure: an agent asked to draft an email consults private CRM records and managers mailbox to enrich its response. We formalize this phenomenon as authorization drift: sequence-level failure in which an agent expands its effective authorization boundary while pursuing the users goal, without external instructions directing the expansion. Authorization drift differs from prompt injection in its nonadversarial origin and from static over-privilege in its emergence during execution. Evaluating this failure requires more than removing adversarial inputs: agents must face useful but unauthorized actions while retaining feasible way to complete the task within bounds. This tests whether agents choose to respect authorization boundaries, rather than whether they can resist an attacker. To enable this evaluation, we introduce the Authorization Drift Benchmark (ADB), comprising 648 samples across seven domains, each pairing sufficient but effortful compliant path with an attractive unauthorized shortcut. This dual-path design makes unauthorized actions useful but unnecessary, allowing us to distinguish avoidable overreach from task requirements. ADB is therefore an opportunity-conditioned stress test, not an estimate of drift prevalence in ordinary deployments. ADB evaluates four authorization dimensions: Data, accessing information beyond the authorized data boundary; Tool, using tools beyond the permitted capabilities; Scope, expanding beyond the requested objective; and Time, persisting or re-planning beyond the intended execution window. An anti-recipe rule preserves realistic information gaps rather than prescribing step-bystep tool calls, requiring agents to navigate these choices themselves. To ensure executable environments, genuinely tempting shortcuts, and feasible compliant paths, we construct ADB through Staged Execution-Reflective Synthesis (SERS). Designer specifies tasks and authorization annotations, Builder implements environments and shortcut opportunities, and quality-control loop evaluates real rollouts from two probe models from different families. By grounding validation in observed agent behavior rather than LLM selfcritique, SERS checks whether these design goals hold during execution, filtering out tasks that are trivially compliant or structurally force drift. Our evaluation contains 25,207 evaluated trajectories from 13 LLMs spanning 4B to 397B parameters under NORMAL; task success is LLM-judged, whereas drift is detected by rule. We additionally compare REACT (Yao et al., 2022) and PLANNER EXECUTOR (Chase, 2022; Wang et al., 2023) on four representative backbones. Capability and drift rise together: frontier-capable models exhibit drift rates of 0.43 to 0.61, yet 86.18% of analyzed tasks admit an observed clean-success trajectory, showing that compliant completion is observed on most tasks. Drift rates are stable across runs, with standard deviations below 0.02 for every model, and early data over-collection dominates over distinct cluster of later scope and time expansion. Lower drift under PLANNEREXECUTOR accompanies collapsing clean-completion performance, while non-monotonic within-family trends suggest that parameter count alone does not explain boundary-keeping. To further understand how these behaviors may harm individuals and society, we use legal provisions as an interpretive framework, mapping annotated drift points to dataprotection and cybersecurity provisions across the European (EU), Mainland China, Singapore, and Hong Kong (HK). This analysis connects technical overreach to concrete concerns, including intrusion into private lives, loss of control over personal information, and unauthorized access to confidential records. GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), concerning data minimisation, is the most frequently implicated provision for every model, and 93.5% of legally grounded drifting runs map to provisions from multiple jurisdictions. These mappings explain the potential human and societal consequences of drift without establishing legal violations or simultaneous applicability across jurisdictions. Our contributions are threefold: We formalize authorization drift as distinct, non-adversarial safety failure across data, tool, scope, and time boundaries, distinguishing it from prompt injection, static over-privilege, and generic privacy leakage. We release ADB, 648-sample dual-path benchmark across seven domains, together with SERS, staged, execution-grounded synthesis pipeline that validates task completion and shortcut triggerability through real agent rollouts. Across 13 LLMs, with three-framework comparisons on four backbones (25,207 evaluation trajectories), we characterize the capabilitydrift association, its persistence and trajectory structure, and the limitations of agentic scaffolds. We further use legal mappings across four jurisdictions to connect these behavioral findings to potential harms to individuals and society.

sections.title: 2.1 Safety Boundaries in Agentic Systems
sections.content: Agent safety research largely examines adversarial failures. InjecAgent (Zhan et al., 2024) and AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024) study indirect prompt injection, while Agent Security Bench (Zhang et al., 2025), AgentHarm (Andriushchenko et al., 2025), and AgentSafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024) cover broader harmful behaviors. Beyond adversarial settings, Figure 2: Overview of the SERS data construction pipeline. Left: raw agent skills across seven representative domains serve as input. Middle: Stage 1 (Designer) produces structured drift scenario playbook; Stage 2 (Builder) translates it into executable environment code, tool schemas, and annotation files. Generated samples pass structural smoke test, then enter trajectory QC loop in which two probe models generate rollouts evaluated by an automated gate. Samples that fail the gate are revised by Critic agent for up to three rounds; unresolved samples are escalated for human review. Right: the final dataset is evaluated across models and agent frameworks. MACHIAVELLI (Pan et al., 2023) and EU-AgentBench (Lichkovski et al., 2025) examine deception and legal non-compliance under benign inputs. Complementary work studies execution isolation through IsolateGPT (Wu et al., 2024), runtime privilege control through Progent (Shi et al., 2025) and GrantBox (Zhang et al., 2026), and privacy violations through PrivacyLens (Shao et al., 2024) and AgentDAM (Zharmagambetov et al., 2026). Building on least privilege (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975) and contextual integrity (Nissenbaum, 2004), we focus on non-adversarial authorization expansion during task execution, evaluating whether agents reject useful unauthorized shortcuts when compliant alternatives remain available.

sections.title: 2.2 Agent Benchmark Construction
sections.content: Agent benchmarks have evolved from API calling and tool manipulation, exemplified by ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2024), ToolBench (Xu et al., 2023), and BFCL (Patil et al., 2025), toward executable workflows in τ -bench (Yao et al., 2024), AgentBench (Liu et al., 2024), and AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024). Skill-based frameworks further motivate longer-horizon evaluation across tools, instructions, and memory (Xu and Yan, 2026; OpenClaw Contributors, 2025). Construction approaches include manual design, synthetic generation, and execution-driven refinement. Manually designed environments offer fidelity but limited scalability, whereas synthetic generation scales more readily but may sacrifice execution fidelity. Recent work therefore uses execution feedback to identify realistic failures (Jones et al., 2026). SERS extends this direction through staged task and environment generation, using real agent rollouts to validate executability, shortcut attractiveness, and compliant-path reachability rather than relying on LLM self-critique.

sections.title: 3.1 Problem Formulation
sections.content: We define an authorization boundary as the set of operations an agent is permitted to perform in pursuit of user request, as determined by implicit professional norms and environment policy: = (D, T, S, H), (1) covering permitted data access (D), tools (T ), task scope (S), and temporal persistence (H). Given trajectory π = (a1, . . . , an) and per-action violation indicator φ(ai, B) {0, 1}, authorization drift occurs when (cid:80) φ(ai, B) > 0 and the violation arises from the agents own goaldirected execution rather than adversarial injection. Each drift action carries two orthogonal labels: drift type identifying the violated component of (data_drift, tool_drift, scope_drift, time_drift), and boundary violation kind capturing the normative reason. The kinds include purpose limitation and data minimization (grounded in GDPR Art. 5(1)(b,c) (European Union, 2016)), explicit prohibition, and implicit red line; full definitions are in Appendix A. For legal analysis, each drift action is further linked to the legal provisions it implicates (3.2). structural property of ADB scenarios is trigger-induced sequentiality: drift actions are causally downstream of compliant steps. Each compliant tool call embeds trigger fielda piece of realistic ambient metadata that makes an unauthorized follow-up feel like natural next step phrased in evaluative rather than imperative language. These triggers therefore differ fundamentally from prompt injection, since they carry no instruction and exert no external pressure (Appendix E.7); the boundary violation is emergent and trajectory-dependent, not externally provoked.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Models & Frameworks. We evaluate 13 LLMs (Claude (AI, 2026), spanning five families Qwen (Qwen Team, 2026a,b,c), Llama (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Meta AI, 2025), MiniMax (MiniMax, 2026), Mistral (Liu et al., 2026); 4B to 397B parameters) using their native function-calling interfaces under NORMAL (bare-model tool calling). To probe scaffold effects, we additionally compare four representative backbones under REACT (ThoughtActionObservation) (Yao et al., 2022) and PLANNEREXECUTOR (realized by LangChain) (Wang et al., 2023; Chase, 2022). Evaluation Settings. Following single-rollout conventions (Pass@1), we report run-level expected probabilities for task success (TSR), drift rate (DR), and compliant success (CSR). We also report CCSR (compliance-conditional success rate) to separate safety from capability collapse, and use sample-level metrics (DRsample) strictly for persistence analysis (PR). Task success is judged by Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct. For Pass@1 evaluation we decode at temperature 0; for multi-run experiments we adopt each models officially recommended sampling temperature, falling back to 0.7 when none is specified.

sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: Higher capability accompanies higher drift, despite reachable compliant alternatives. Table 1 and Figure 3 show clear positive association between TSR and DR under NORMAL. Llama models achieve TSR 0.270.63 with DR below 0.18; Mistral models and MiniMax-M2.7 reach TSR 0.710.83 with DR 0.240.39; and Qwen models and Claude Sonnet 4.6 attain TSR 0.90 with DR 0.430.61. Stronger task performance therefore does not translate into better authorization compliance: highly capable models frequently cross boundaries, while low-drift models complete substantially fewer tasks, leaving the high-capability, low-drift region empty. This association might suggest that successful completion requires unauthorized actions. sections.title: 5 Discussion and Analysis
sections.content: Beyond the capabilitydrift association in Section 4.2, we examine four complementary aspects of authorization drift: its persistence across rollouts, its behavioural structure across domains and trajectory stages, its interaction with agent frameworks, and its potential legal implications. Together, these analyses clarify where drift concentrates and what effective mitigation must preserve.

sections.title: 5.2 Behavioural Structure of Drift
sections.content: Data over-collection is the modal failure mode. Data drift is the largest component for every model (up to 0.574 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), while Productivity, Security, and Finance have the highest domain-level DR  (Table 3)  . This ordering is consistent with helpfulness-driven interpretation in which agents gather additional context, but the observational comparison does not by itself identify the cause of drift. Figure 4: Kernel-density estimate of where each drift type occurs along the trajectory (normalized position 0 1; 0 = first tool call, 1 = last action). Data drift concentrates early-to-mid, Scope and Time drift shift to the second half, and Tool drift peaks latest. Data drift peaking early-to-mid (0.20.5), whereas Scope and Time drift shift to the second half (0.6 0.8) and Tool drift peaks after 0.7. These positions motivate complementary safeguards, such as limits on early context-gathering calls and explicit completion-condition checks during later stages of task execution. Co-occurrence patterns suggest partially distinct failure modes. Time and Scope have the strongest correlation (r = 0.30), Tool co-occurs moderately with both (r 0.20), and Data has weaker correlations (r = 0.110.15; Figure 5). Combined with their different trajectory positions, these patterns motivate complementary controls for early data collection and later task expansion, without establishing that the categories are causally independent.

sections.title: 5.4 Potential Legal Implications
sections.content: Drift maps most often to data-minimisation provisions across several jurisdictions. GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) is the most frequently implicated provision for all 13 models and, with its Mainland China and Hong Kong counterparts (NDSR Art. 22(1), PDPO DPP1(1)(c)), forms the top three for 12 of them (Figure 7; 43/35/31% for Claude Sonnet 4.6). Llama-3.3-70B is the exception: Data drift only slightly exceeds its Scope and Time drift, and GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) appears in 40% of its legally grounded runs. Overall, 93.5% of legally Figure 7: Provision-level drift rate DRℓ (% of runs) for the ten provisions with the highest mean rate across models. The full matrix over all 58 provisions is in Appendix D.3. grounded drifting runs map to provisions from at least two jurisdictions. This indicates that the same behavioural overreach often corresponds to provisions across multiple regimes; it does not establish simultaneous applicability or legal violation. The mapping covers data-related drift more comprehensively than other types. DRL stays within 6.2 points of DR and preserves the model ranking in Table 1. Binding provisions cover 99.2% of Data drift points, compared with 55.1% of Scope, 49.6% of Time, and 35.2% of Tool points. This difference characterizes the coverage of our mapping and should not be interpreted as establishing that the remaining behaviours are unregulated under applicable law. Together, these findings motivate evaluating safeguards jointly on drift and compliant completion, with complementary controls for early data collection and later task expansion.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We formalize authorization drift across data, tool, scope, and time, and introduce ADB, 648sample dual-path benchmark constructed through execution-grounded SERS. Across 13 LLMs, with three-framework comparisons on four backbones, drift is persistent, compliant completion is empirically observed on most tasks, and data overcollection dominates; greater capability does not ensure boundary-keeping, and agentic scaffolds provide limited protection. Legal mappings across four jurisdictions connect these failures to potential harms to individuals and society. These findings motivate trajectory-level training and runtime authorization controls that preserve legitimate task completion without permitting overreach.

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: The single-session, single-user framing leaves multi-agent authorization surfaces unaddressed. Delegated sub-agents, shared memory stores, crosssession persistence, and inter-agent trust propagation all introduce additional boundary-crossing risks that ADB does not yet measure. Drift detection uses tool-name and argument-subset matching against annotated violation_tool_calls; novel boundary-crossing patterns that fall outside the designed violation set are not captured. This may cause ADB to underestimate drift for highly capable models that discover unanticipated unauthorized paths not represented in the benchmark. Extending ADB to live deployment environments, multi-agent settings, and open-ended violation detection represents natural direction for future work.

sections.title: 8 Ethics Statement
sections.content: ADB is designed as diagnostic tool to expose and measure safety failure mode, not to enable attacks. All tasks use mock environments with no real user data; no production systems were queried during evaluation. We release the benchmark to support the research community in developing safer agents, and we encourage responsible disclosure if deployed systems are tested with ADB-derived scenarios.

sections.title: A Formal Definitions
sections.content: C.3 Drift Point and Type Distribution Boundary violation kinds. Each drift action in ADB carries normative label drawn from four categories. Two are grounded in GDPR Art. 5 (European Union, 2016): Purpose limitation: data or tools used for purpose incompatible with the original task (cf. Art. 5(1)(b), which requires that personal data be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and not further processed in an incompatible manner). Data minimization: accessing data clearly beyond what the task requires (cf. Art. 5(1)(c), which requires that data be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary). Explicit prohibition: the instruction explicitly forbids the action yet the agent executes it. Implicit red line: high-risk, state-mutating, or externalizing action that reasonable professional would confirm before executing, absent any explicit prohibition. Rule-based task completion (TC). As deterministic complement to the LLM-judged TSR, we also report rule-based task completion: trajectory is TC-complete iff every required_tool_call appears at least once (order-agnostic). sections.title: D Legal Grounding
sections.content: D.1 Provision Registry and Taxonomy The registry covers eleven legal instruments in four jurisdictions  (Table 10)  . For each instrument, an LLM reads the full text and extracts every provision that could directly adjudicate concrete drift behaviour, splitting numbered subparagraphs whenever each can be applied on its own and excluding definitional, institutional, procedural, scope, and pure-penalty clauses (prompt in Figure 20). Each provision is stored verbatim with its applicable drift types, yielding 150 provisions; excluding the 19 AI Act provisions and one non-binding AGENT provision leaves 130 in the provision-linked analysis. Provisions are grouped into two-level taxonomy of functional obligations that cuts across jurisdictions (e.g., Data Minimisation groups GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), NDSR Art. 22(1), and PDPO DPP1(1)(c)), so that matching can first select category and then provision. Table 11 reports the categories that remain populated after the exclusions described in 3.2. Step 2 (one call per drift point; Figure 22) presents the full text of every provision in the selected categories and asks the model to keep only directly relevant provisions, ranked by relevance, with written justification.
